name: Don Nomura
status: Still a public figure at 69: his memoir about 34 years as an agent came out in July 2026. His current clients, title and company website could not be confirmed. Recent big Japanese moves to MLB (for example Roki Sasaki) were handled by other agents.
summary: The agent who got Hideo Nomo out of Japan in 1995 by finding a gap in the rules, then did it again with Hideki Irabu (1997) and Alfonso Soriano (1998). Those three fights forced Japanese and American baseball to create the posting system. Half American, half Japanese, stepson of the famous manager Katsuya Nomura, he was for years the most disliked man in Japanese baseball offices.
quick_facts: 17 May 1957, Tokyo, as Donald Engel (American father, Japanese mother)
Stepson of Katsuya Nomura, the legendary catcher and manager; his mother was the TV personality Sachiyo Nomura

Married in 1981 and moved to Los Angeles with his wife that December. At least one child: a daughter born in the early 1980s. Names and any other children are not public. His mother had several grandchildren across her three sons.
Yakult Swallows farm team 1978 to 1981; never played a first-team game
Moved to Los Angeles in 1981; in 1989 bought half of the Salinas Spurs, a low minor-league club in California
KDN Sports, Los Angeles (founded 1992 or 1993; sources differ)
Hideo Nomo 1995, Hideki Irabu 1997, Alfonso Soriano 1998, Yu Darvish 2012 (with Arn Tellem)
American agent Arn Tellem and lawyer Jean Afterman

sections.title: In short
sections.intro: Nomura did not win by being friendly with clubs. He won by reading the rulebook more carefully than the people who wrote it, and by being willing to be hated. He could do it because he stood between two worlds: he knew Japanese baseball from the inside (through his stepfather and his own failed playing career) and American baseball law through partners in Los Angeles.

cells: Born in Tokyo to an American father and a Japanese mother. His parents divorce when he is about six.
Expelled from an international school in Tokyo for fighting; plays college baseball in California; takes Japanese citizenship and the Nomura name when Katsuya Nomura adopts him.
Infielder in the Yakult Swallows farm system. Released without reaching the first team.
Moves to Los Angeles: odd jobs, interpreting, then property.
Buys 50% of the Salinas Spurs (California League) for about $300,000 and fills the team with Japanese players. It loses money and games.
Sells his Spurs share. Mac Suzuki asks him to be his agent: his first client. Suzuki signs with the Seattle Mariners in 1993.
Late 1994
Meets Hideo Nomo. Finds that the rules only bind 'active' players, and gets the Japanese commissioner's office to confirm it by fax on 9 Dec.
Walks into Nomo's contract meeting with Kintetsu and is told to leave.
Nomo signs with the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Sports Illustrated reports that all 12 Japanese clubs have shut him out and that the Hiroshima Carp are suing him for $1 million over pitcher Robinson Checo.
Hideki Irabu: Lotte gives his rights to San Diego; Irabu will only play for the Yankees; Nomura fights and Irabu gets to New York.
Alfonso Soriano 'retires' from Hiroshima; MLB declares him a free agent on 13 July. In December the posting system is created.
Posting talks between Hisashi Iwakuma and Oakland fail; Nomura blames the club. Iwakuma changes agents in 2011.
Jan 2012
Yu Darvish signs with the Texas Rangers for six years and $60 million; Nomura and Arn Tellem are his agents.
Nov 2019

The Japanese entertainment company Amuse announces it will buy 51% of a California holding company to enter the athlete-agent business. Japanese Wikipedia says this was the purchase of KDN; not confirmed from a primary document.
July 2026
Publishes a memoir with KADOKAWA about 34 years as an agent, with chapters on Nomo and Irabu and proposals for Japanese baseball.

parts.heading: The defence
rows: Everything he did for Nomo was legal and confirmed in advance by the Japanese commissioner's office.
https://japanesebaseball.com/writers/display.gsp?id=34924
Players had almost no rights in 1994: no agents, and many years before free agency. His cases forced the leagues to build a proper route, the posting system.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posting_system
Nomo stood by him: in the first Kintetsu meeting he asked Nomura to come into the room with him.
https://bunshun.jp/articles/-/90543
After the Irabu case the American players' union moved to stop players being traded like that without their consent.
https://japanball.com/articles-features/japanese-baseball-historical-profiles/negotiations-nomo-and-nomura-how-one-agent-changed-the-landscape-of-international-baseball/
His publisher credits him with opening the road to the majors for several Japanese players.
https://books.bunshun.jp/ud/book/num/9784163556802
The loophole he used is closed. Since December 1998 the normal route is the posting system or full free agency.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posting_system
Agents are now normal in Japanese baseball, so his old role as the lone outsider no longer exists.
https://bunshun.jp/articles/-/90543
His last confirmed headline deal was Darvish in 2012. No current client could be confirmed by name for 2020 to 2026; his companies say they have about 60 athletes in total (see the next chapter).
https://www.foxnews.com/sports/darvish-texas-agree-to-60m-6-yr-deadline-deal
He is still heard in public: a 2020 interview, a 2026 memoir, and Japanese newspaper pieces in November 2026 recalling his time as interpreter for pitcher Yutaka Enatsu's 1985 try at the majors.
https://japanball.com/articles-features/chatter-up/baseball-agent-don-nomura-talks-nomo-and-negotiating/
No public comment by him on Ohtani, Sasaki or today's posting rules was found.

parts.text: Short answer: at 69 he is still in the business, but he no longer owns or runs it alone. His agency is now majority-owned by a big Japanese advertising group, and he spends visible time on his memoir and on commentary. Searched 21 Nov 2026.

cells: His company

His agency was first sold to the Japanese entertainment company Amuse (announced 2019). On 26 Aug 2025 the advertising group Hakuhodo bought 66.7% of the holding company, 'Amuse Sports Holdings (CEO: Don Nomura)', and renamed it HAKUHODO Athlete Solution.
✅ Hakuhodo press release
His job title

Not confirmed. The press release says a Hakuhodo executive, Tetsu Toyoshita, became president and CEO of all three companies. It does not say what post Nomura holds now. A job-listing site and Japanese Wikipedia still call him representative director of Athlete Solution; they may be out of date.
🟡 Sources disagree
The business he built

Athlete Solution (Tokyo): about 40 athletes in baseball, soccer, rugby, table tennis, basketball and padel. Athlete Solution USA (Los Angeles): about 20 athletes, including foreign players in MLB. No names are given.
✅ Hakuhodo press release
Writing
His memoir フィールドから契約へ ('From the Field to the Contract: 34 years as an agent') came out in 2026. Sports Navi has been publishing extracts under his name from September to November 2026.
Speaking out
A YouTube video linked from those extracts has him arguing against cutting high-school baseball games to 7 innings, and for pitch-count limits. He also has an X account (@donnomura).
✅ Link seen; video not watched
Soccer
Japanese Wikipedia lists him as a registered intermediary (agent) with the Japan Football Association.
🟡 Wikipedia only
Where he lives

Not confirmed. He moved to Los Angeles in 1981 and his companies have offices in Los Angeles and in Minato, Tokyo. In a radio interview he said his work is split half and half between Japan and the USA. No reliable source states his home city today, and a private address would not be recorded here anyway.
⚪ Not confirmed

parts.heading: His own family
rows: He married in 1981 and moved to Los Angeles with his wife in December that year.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Nomura

He has at least one child, a daughter born in the early 1980s. When money ran out he sent his wife and baby daughter back to Japan and lived in his car in Los Angeles; by 1985 he could rent an apartment and bring them back.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Nomura

His mother Sachiyo had several grandchildren from her three sons (Don, Kenny and Katsunori). The only one named in public for baseball work is Kenny's daughter, who works for the Los Angeles Angels. So she is his niece, not his child.
https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/野村沙知代
Not found: his wife's name, how many children he has in total, or what they do. They are private people, so nothing more is recorded here.

parts.text: My reading: he followed the same path as his old partner Arn Tellem's firm. A founder-led agency was sold to a larger company that wants athletes for marketing and media. Compare the chapter on Wasserman.

cells: Arn Tellem
American lawyer and agent (born 1954); later a top basketball agent and vice chairman of the Detroit Pistons. Also represented Hideki Matsui.
The US-based agent Nomura worked with; checked the contract clause. His Wikipedia page credits him with finding the loophole, which other accounts give to Nomura.
Jean Afterman
American lawyer; joined the New York Yankees in 2001 as assistant general manager.
As Nomura's lawyer she went through the translated rules and league letters and helped find the 'active players only' gap. Also fought the Irabu case.

parts.text: Wasserman is a large American sports agency (founded 2002 by Casey Wasserman, now renamed THE TEAM). Short answer: Nomura never worked for Wasserman and no source says Wasserman owned any part of his company. The link is a partnership, deal by deal, that ran through one man: Arn Tellem. Searched 21 Nov 2026.

cells: Nomo's Dodgers deal: Nomura works with American agent Arn Tellem, who then ran his own firm, Tellem and Associates.
None yet. Wasserman did not exist until 2002.
Tellem's firm is bought by SFX (1999). In 2006 Wasserman Media Group buys his basketball and baseball business, and he becomes its vice chairman.
Nomura's long-time American partner is now a Wasserman executive.
Yu Darvish is represented jointly by 'Arn Tellem of Wasserman Media Group and Don Nomura'. He signs with Texas for 6 years, $60 million.
✅ The clearest link: one client shared between Nomura and Wasserman.
Tellem leaves the agent business to join the Detroit Pistons' owners. In December Kenta Maeda hires Adam Katz of Wasserman for his MLB talks; Nomura's publisher also credits Nomura with Maeda's move.
🟡 Probably a second shared client, but no single report names both men together.
2017 (reported 2019)

A Japanese weekly magazine (FLASH) reports that Darvish ended his contract with Nomura in 2017, angry about a separate paid contract between Nomura and Asics that he had not been told about. One-sided report; no public confirmation from Darvish or Nomura was found.
⚪ If true, the shared client stayed with Wasserman and left Nomura.
2020 onward
Darvish's agent is Joel Wolfe, head of baseball at Wasserman, who also represents many later Japanese stars (Yamamoto, Senga, Seiya Suzuki).
Wasserman became the main agency for Japanese players in MLB; Nomura is not named in these deals.

In his memoir Nomura has a section on what he learned from Tellem, and writes that sharing a client among several agents is better than fighting over one. Baseball-Reference lists Darvish's agents as 'THE·TEAM; previously Arn Tellem & Don Nomura' (THE TEAM is Wasserman's new company name, per Wikipedia).
His own explanation of why he partnered with a big American firm.

parts.text: My reading: this is the same 'local partner plus big foreign firm' pattern seen with Japanese soccer agents. Nomura had the trust of the Japanese player; Tellem and Wasserman had the American lawyers, team contacts and scale. When Tellem left in 2015, the personal bridge went with him, and Wasserman's own agent Joel Wolfe now deals with Japanese players directly.

rows: See also the full page on Wasserman (now THE·TEAM): its Japanese players, business model and the LA 2028 Olympics link.
https://anishimori123.github.io/News/agents/wasserman.html
An outsider with inside knowledge is powerful. He knew how Japanese clubs think, but did not depend on them for his living.
Rules are written by people, and people leave gaps. He looked for what the text said, not what custom said.
Being right is not the same as being liked. He paid for these wins with years of being shut out in Japan.
The agent needs the right client. The plan only worked because Nomo was calm under attack and good enough to succeed at once.
